uncited: - Input: A global list of $N$ 3D Gaussians, each defined by position $\mathbf{p}_i$, covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}_i$, opacity $\alpha_i$, spherical harmonic coefficients $\mathbf{c}_i$, and scaling $\mathbf{s}_i$.
The global Gaussian list is partitioned into $K$ subsets $\mathcal{G}_0, \dots, \mathcal{G}_{K-1}$, where $\mathcal{G}_k$ resides on GPU $k$.
Each subset contains a contiguous block of Gaussian attributes.
The partitioning is static or dynamic based on scene geometry or load balancing.
**Partitioning:** Divide the $N$ Gaussians into $K$ disjoint sets $\mathcal{G}_k$ assigned to GPU $k$.
**Local Rendering:** Each GPU $k$ renders the scene using only Gaussians in $\mathcal{G}_k$.
This produces a partial color image $\mathbf{I}_k$ and partial transmittance/depth information.

**Inter-GPU Communication:** At partition boundaries, GPUs exchange necessary intermediate data (e.g., transmittance $T$ or accumulated color contributions) to ensure correct alpha-blending across the global scene.
This step resolves dependencies where a Gaussian on GPU $j$ occludes or is occluded by a Gaussian on GPU $k$.
**Global Composite:** The partial images are combined to form the final rendered image $\mathbf{I}$ for each training view.
**Loss Computation:** Compute the loss $\mathcal{L}$ between $\mathbf{I}$ and the ground truth image.
**Gradient Distribution:** Gradients $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}$ are computed and distributed back to the respective GPUs based on which Gaussian contributed to the loss.
**Parameter Update:** Each GPU updates its local subset of Gaussian parameters using the received gradients.
- **Occlusion Across Partitions:** If a Gaussian on GPU $j$ occludes a Gaussian on GPU $k$, the alpha-blending order must be respected.
- **Load Imbalance:** Uneven distribution of Gaussians or complex geometry on specific GPUs can lead to bottlenecks.
- **Communication Overhead:** Inter-GPU communication latency can dominate computation time if not optimized.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot V)$ per iteration, where $N$ is the number of Gaussians and $V$ is the number of views, distributed across $K$ GPUs.
Communication overhead adds $O(K \cdot B)$, where $B$ is the boundary size.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(N/K)$ per GPU, enabling training of scenes with $N \gg \text{VRAM}_{\text{GPU}}$.
- **Limitations:** Communication overhead; complex implementation; requires high-bandwidth interconnects (e.g., NVLink) for optimal performance.
- **When to Use:** Large-scale scenes (e.g., urban environments, large indoor spaces) that exceed single-GPU memory.
- **When Not to Use:** Small scenes; single-GPU setups; scenarios where communication latency is high.
Grendel-GS was introduced as part of the effort to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to massive scenes.
